en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 133, the Mahākaccānabhaddekaratta Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapoda Monastery.
Then, as the night was drawing to a close, the Venerable Samiddhi rose and went to the hot spring to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs in the hot spring and emerged, he stood there dressed in a single robe, drying his limbs.
Then, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Tapodā Park, approached the Venerable Samiddhi. Having approached, she stood to one side.
Standing there, that deity said this to the Venerable Samiddhi:
“Bhikkhu, do you remember the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’?
“I do not, friend, remember the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night.
But do you, friend, remember the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’?”
“Monk, I too do not remember the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night.
But do you, monk, remember the verses of ‘One Fortunate Night’?
“I do not remember them, friend; I do not remember the verses of ‘One Fortunate Night.’”
“But do you, friend, remember the *Bhaddekaratta* verses?
“I too, bhikkhu, do not remember the *Bhaddekaratta* verses.
Learn, bhikkhu, both the summary and the exposition of the *Bhaddekaratta*.”
“Master the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night,’ bhikkhu;
memorize the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night,’ bhikkhu.
The summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’ are beneficial, bhikkhu, and they pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life.”
Thus spoke that deity.
Having said this, she vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
"Just now, Bhante, having risen at the time of dawn, I went to the bathing pool to bathe my limbs.
Having bathed my limbs in the pool and come out, I stood there wearing a single robe, rubbing my limbs dry."
Then, venerable sir, at the end of the night, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Tapodā Park, approached me; having approached, she stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to me:
“‘Bhikkhu, do you remember the summary and the exposition of the Bhaddekaratta?
When this was said, venerable sir, I said to that deity:
‘I do not, friend, remember the summary and the exposition of the Bhaddekaratta.’”
“But do you, friend, remember the summary and the exposition of the *Bhaddekaratta*?
“I too, bhikkhu, do not remember the summary and the exposition of the *Bhaddekaratta*.
But do you, bhikkhu, remember the verses of the *Bhaddekaratta*?”
“I do not remember the verses of the Single Excellent Night, friend.
But do you, friend, remember the verses of the Single Excellent Night?
“I too, bhikkhu, do not remember the verses of the Single Excellent Night.”
"Learn, monk, the summary and the exposition of 'One Fortunate Night';
master, monk, the summary and the exposition of 'One Fortunate Night';
bear in mind, monk, the summary and the exposition of 'One Fortunate Night'."
“Bhikkhu, this recitation and exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night,’ which is connected with the goal and fundamental to the holy life,” said that deity, Bhante.
Having said this, she vanished right there.
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the summary and the exposition of ‘One Who Has Had a Single Excellent Night.
“In that case, bhikkhu, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Samiddhi replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“One should not pursue the past,
nor should one long for the future.”
That which is past is abandoned;
that which is future has not yet been reached;
and as for the phenomenon that is present—
Therein, one sees with insight;
the wise person should cultivate that which is unshakable and unshakeable.
"Today itself the task must be undertaken with diligence;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no agreement with it."
By Death with his great army.
One who dwells thus,
ardent and untiring by day and night—
“The Sage who is at peace indeed declares that this is ‘One Fortunate Night’.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us this brief summary, without analyzing the meaning in detail."
“One should not pursue the past,
nor long for the future;
what is past has been relinquished.”
And that which has not yet been reached, the future;
and whatever phenomenon is present—
whosoever discerns these in their respective places;
That which is unshakable and unagitated—
the wise person should cultivate that. One should exert oneself this very day in what is to be done.
Who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no agreement with that Death who possesses a vast army.
One who dwells thus,
ardent and untiring by day and night,
is indeed called "Bhaddekaratta."
“The Sage declares what is wholesome.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: “Who could analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
And then it occurred to them: [that the Venerable Sāriputta might do so].
“This Venerable Mahākaccāna is indeed praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by wise companions in the holy life.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
Let us approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna regarding this matter.”
Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:

"Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One, having given us a brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling: [‘Bhikkhus, I shall not teach you the Dhamma by way of the specific and the general...’]"
“One should not pursue the past...
That indeed is called ‘one who has had a single auspicious night.’”
"The Sage declares it to the virtuous.
Then, friend Kaccāna, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this occurred to us:
"Friends, the Blessed One has given us this brief summary of the teaching and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling."
“One should not pursue the past...
That indeed is called ‘one who has had a single auspicious night.’”
“The Sage declares what is true.
“Who, friend Kaccāna, might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, friends, it occurred to us:
‘This venerable Mahākaccāna is indeed praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates.
The venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
Suppose we were to approach the venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter.’
"Venerable Mahākaccāna, please explain this. "Friend,
it is just as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by a great tree standing there possessed of heartwood, and having bypassed the root and the trunk, were to look for heartwood in the branches and foliage."
you would think it should be sought after;
in the same way, friends, while the Teacher is present before you, you bypass that Blessed One and think that this matter should be asked of us.

For that Blessed One, friends, knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
“Indeed, it would have been the right time for you to ask the Blessed One about this matter yourselves, so that you might remember it exactly as the Blessed One explained it.

“Certainly, friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. He is the embodiment of vision, the embodiment of knowledge, the embodiment of Dhamma, the embodiment of Brahma. He is the speaker, the one who sets things in motion, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
Indeed, it would have been the right time for us to ask the Blessed One about this matter ourselves.”
"We shall remember it exactly as the Blessed One explains it.
Moreover, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates;
the Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed."
“Let the venerable Mahākaccāna explain this, not making it a burden.
“Therefore, friends, listen and attend closely; I shall speak,” he said.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Mahākaccāna.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:
"Friends, regarding that brief summary which the Blessed One recited for us and then, without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
'One should not pursue the past...'"
"That indeed is called 'the one fortunate night,' so the peaceful Sage has declared."
"Friends, regarding this brief summary taught by the Blessed One whose meaning has not been analyzed in detail, I understand its meaning in detail as follows:
And how, friends, does one pursue the past?
'Such was my eye in the past, such were the forms,' thus one pursues the past."
Therein, consciousness is bound by desire and lust; because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it. Delighting in it, one pursues the past:
"Thus was my ear in the past, thus were sounds... ...pe...
"Thus was my nose in the past, thus were odors..."
"Thus was my tongue in the past, thus were tastes...
Thus was my body in the past, thus were tangibles...
Thus was my mind in the past, thus were mental phenomena."
Therein, consciousness is bound by desire and lust; because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in that. Delighting in it, one pursues the past.
In this way, friend, one pursues the past.
And how, friend, does one not pursue the past?
"Thus my eye was in the past, and thus were forms"—in this regard, consciousness is not bound by desire and lust;
because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in it; not delighting in it, one does not pursue the past.
"Thus my ear was in the past, and thus were sounds"... [and so on].
"Such was my nose in the past, such were the odors...
such was my tongue in the past, such were the flavors...
such was my body in the past, such were the tangibles..."
"Such was my mind regarding the past:

'Such were the phenomena'—in this regard, consciousness is not bound by desire and lust; because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in that; not delighting in it, one does not pursue the past.
It is in this way, friend, that one does not pursue the past."
And how, friends, does one long for the future?

Thinking, "May my eye be such in the future," and "may forms be such"—one sets the mind on the attainment of what has not yet been attained; conditioned by that mental aspiration, one delights in it; delighting in it, one longs for the future.
"Thus may my ear exist in the future time, thus sounds... ...
"Thus may my nose exist in the future time, thus odors... ...
"Thus may my tongue exist in the future time, thus tastes..."
"May my body be thus in the future," "may my tangible objects be thus," ...

"may my mind be thus in the future," "may my mental phenomena be thus"—for the sake of obtaining what has not yet been obtained, he fixes his mind upon it; conditioned by that mental fixation, he delights in it; delighting in it, he longs for the future.
In this way, friends, one looks forward to the future.
And how, friends, does one not look forward to the future?
"May my eye be thus in the future time," and "may forms be thus"—[this is how one looks forward].

He does not direct his mind toward the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired; because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in it; not delighting in it, he does not long for the future.
Thus: "May my ear exist in the future as such sounds... ... "May my nose exist in the future as such odors... [and so on].
"May my tongue be thus in the future," "tastes be thus...
"May my body be thus in the future," "tangibles be thus...
"May my mind be thus in the future," "mental phenomena be thus"—...

One does not direct the mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained; because of this lack of mental aspiration, one does not delight in it; not delighting in it, one does not long for the future.
It is in this way, friend, that one does not long for the future.
And how, friend, is one carried away by present phenomena?
Friends, the eye and forms—both of these are present.

If consciousness is bound to desire and lust for that which is present, then because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it; delighting in it, one is swept away by present phenomena.
And, friends, the ear and sounds...
[and so on] ...the nose and odors...
the tongue and tastes... [and so on].
And whatever body, friends, and whatever tangibles...
and whatever mind, friends, and whatever mental phenomena—
both of these are present.

If consciousness is bound to desire and lust for that which is present, then because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it; delighting in it, one is swept away by present phenomena.
In this way, friend, one is swept away by present phenomena.
And how, friend, is one not swept away by present phenomena?
Friends, the eye and forms—both these are present.

If consciousness is not bound to that which is present by desire and lust, then because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in it; not delighting in it, one is not swept away by present phenomena.
And, friends, whatever ear and whatever sounds...
whatever nose and whatever odors...
whatever tongue and whatever tastes... [and so forth].
And whatever body, friends, and whatever tangible objects...
and whatever mind, friends, and whatever mental phenomena—
both of these are present.

If consciousness is not bound by desire and lust for that which is present, then because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in it. Not delighting in it, one is not swept away by phenomena that are present.
It is in this way, friend, that one is not swept away by phenomena that are present.
Now, friends, regarding that brief summary which the Blessed One recited and then, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:
“One should not pursue the past...
That indeed is called ‘one who has had a single auspicious night.’”
“The Sage explains it to the virtuous.
Regarding this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which has not yet been analyzed in detail, this is how I understand its meaning in detail.
However, if you wish, venerable friends, you should approach the Blessed One himself and inquire about this matter further.
“Just as the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.
Then those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and delighted in the Venerable Mahākaccāna’s words, rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One.
Having approached the Blessed One, they paid homage to him and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, when the Blessed One had given us a brief summary and, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
‘One should not pursue the past...’”
That indeed is called 'the one auspicious night' by the peaceful Sage."
“Venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred to us:
‘Friends, the Blessed One has given us this brief summary of the teaching and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling:
“One should not pursue the past... [and so forth].”
One should not long for the future;
for that which is past is abandoned,
and that which is future has not yet arrived.
And whoever discerns, here and there, the phenomenon that is present—
unshakable and unshakeable—
Knowing this, one should cultivate it.
Diligence is to be practiced this very day;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no compact with that Death who possesses a great army;
[we do not fear] one who dwells thus, ardent.
“Undertaking this day and night without sloth— this, indeed,
the peaceful Sage calls ‘One Fortunate Night.’”
"Who, indeed, might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, Bhante, it occurred to us:
"This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.

What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and inquire about this matter? Then, venerable sir, we approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, inquired about this matter.
“Venerable sir, the meaning has been analyzed for us by the Venerable Mahākaccāna in these ways, with these phrases, and with these syllables.
“Bhikkhus, Mahākaccāna is wise; Mahākaccāna has great wisdom.
If you had questioned me about this matter, I too would have explained it in exactly the same way as it was explained by Mahākaccāna.”
"And this, indeed, is its meaning. And thus you should remember it.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse to Mahākaccāna on the Single Excellent Night is finished; this is the third.
